newsitem.title: RUSSIA: UES seen sparking Russian corporate bonds.
newsitem.headline: UES seen sparking Russian corporate bonds.

text.p: Utility Unified Energy System's planned convertible Eurobond is likely to spark the development of a corporate bond market as firms seek to benefit from Russia's new debt rating, analysts said on Thursday.

The UES issue, which privatisation minister Alfred Kokh said would be convertible into 7.5 percent of its shares, follows the allocation of a sovereign credit rating to Russia earlier this month and is likely to be the first of many.
"This is the first of a series of Russian non-sovereign Eurobonds that are already in the pipeline for 1997," said Robert Devane, head of fixed income at Troika-Dialog.
"By the end of 1997 we will see enough Eurobonds to form a purely Russian portfolio," he added.
Kokh told reporters national power company UES (RAO Yedinaya Energeticheskaya Sistema in Russian) would issue the bond in the first half of December but gave no details.

The State Property Committee, chaired by Kokh, said in September it would sell 7.5 percent of UES through convertible bonds aimed partly at foreign investors. The stake would be worth some $260 million at current share prices.
UES is some 60 percent state-owned and the government intends to keep 51 percent until the end of 1998.
Devane said this would allow UES to benefit from Russia's recently-awarded credit ratings for its own Eurobond debut.
Standard & Poors assigned Russia BB- and Moody's gave it Ba2. Both are high speculative grades.
"What dealers and investors will be trying to decide is what would be an appropriate credit spread for UES. But there are enough reference points in emerging markets utilities," Devane added.

Corporate bonds have yet to take off in Russia. Analysts cite lack of transparency in company finances, a history of currency instability and high interest rates and the appeal of other instruments as obstacles to its development.

"Treasury bills (GKOs) are sucking up a lot of free assets. The government would like to have a bond market but they have their own problems trying to get money for GKOs," said Rinaco Plus fixed income analyst Peter Kisler.

Devane said it would have been impossible in the past to issue a fixed-coupon bond in Russia and that launching one with a floating or adjustable coupon would be too complex for the available infrastructure.
Russia's biggest oil company LUKoil, beginning last year, sold 460,000 bonds convertible into 78.2 million shares. Atlantic Richfield Co bought some 335,000.

State-owned RAO Vysokoskorostnye Magistrali, planning to build a high-speed rail link between Moscow and St Petersburg, has made two one-year issues to raise 360 billion roubles but the bonds were government-backed.
Kisler said UES could raise funds in the Euromarkets more cheaply than at home.
Devane said there was no track record for a domestic bond issue but investors would have benchmarks by which to judge a Euro-issue.

Both analysts said there was also a fashion element involved in the issue. "It is the same trend as with American Depositary Receipts. A bunch of companies issued ADRs. Why not issue Eurobonds?" said Kisler.
Devane said that, in common with the planned sovereign Euroissue, some of the bond's attractiveness would also derive from the novelty value.

However, it would also benefit from the recent inclusion of Russia in International Finance Corporation emerging market indices which would lead some portfolio managers to increase their allocation to Russia.
